Rigid affine surfaces with isomorphic 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}-cylindersThanks: This research was partialy supported by ANR Grant "BirPol" ANR-11-JS01-004-01.

Adrien Dubouloz Address: IMB UMR5584, CNRS, Univ. Bourgogne Franche-Comté, F-21000 Dijon, France. Email address: adrien.dubouloz@u-bourgogne.fr
Abstract.

We construct families of smooth affine surfaces with pairwise non isomorphic 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cylinders but whose 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}-cylinders are all isomorphic. These arise as complements of cuspidal hyperplane sections of smooth projective cubic surfaces.

Key words and phrases:
Rigid surfaces, Cancellation Problem
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
14R05, 14R25, 14E07

Introduction

The Zariski Cancellation Problem, which asks whether two, say smooth affine, algebraic varieties XX and YY with isomorphic cylinders X×𝔸nX\times\mathbb{A}^{n} and Y×𝔸nY\times\mathbb{A}^{n} for some n≥1n\geq 1 are isomorphic themselves, has been studied very actively during the past decades culminating recently with a negative solution in dimension 33 and positive characteristic for the case X=𝔸3X=\mathbb{A}^{3} [7]. The situation in the complex case, and more generally over any algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, is more contrasted: cancellation is known to hold for curves [1] and for 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2} [6], but many counter-examples in every dimension higher or equal to 22 have been discovered (see [14] for a survey), inspired by the two pioneering constructions of Hochster [8] and Danielewski [2].

Essentially all known families are counter-examples to the cancellation of 11-dimensional cylinders which arise from the existence of nontrivial decompositions of certain locally trivial 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}-bundles over a base scheme ZZ. Namely, Hochster type constructions rely on the existence of non free, 11-stably free, projective modules which in geometric term correspond to non trivial decompositions of the trivial bundle Z×𝔸r+1→ZZ\times\mathbb{A}^{r+1}\rightarrow Z into a trivial 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle over a nontrivial vector bundle E→ZE\rightarrow Z of rank r≥1r\geq 1. For every such bundle, the varieties X=EX=E and Y=Z×𝔸rY=Z\times\mathbb{A}^{r} have isomorphic cylinders X×𝔸1X\times\mathbb{A}^{1} and Y×𝔸1Y\times\mathbb{A}^{1}, and one then gets a counter-example to the cancellation problem whenever XX and YY, which by definition are non isomorphic as schemes over ZZ, are actually non isomorphic as abstract algebraic varieties [10]. In contrast, Danielewski type constructions usually involve non trivial decompositions of a principal homogeneous 𝔾a2\mathbb{G}_{a}^{2}-bundle W→ZW\rightarrow Z into pairs W→X→ZW\rightarrow X\rightarrow Z and W→Y→ZW\rightarrow Y\rightarrow Z consisting of trivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-bundles over nontrivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-bundles X→ZX\rightarrow Z and Y→ZY\rightarrow Z with affine total spaces, with the property that WW is isomorphic to the fiber product W=X×ZYW=X\times_{Z}Y. The isomorphism X×𝔸1≃W≃Y×𝔸1X\times\mathbb{A}^{1}\simeq W\simeq Y\times\mathbb{A}^{1} is granted by definition, and similarly as in the previous type of construction, one obtains counter-examples to the cancellation problem as soon as XX and YY are not isomorphic as abstract varieties.

Non-cancellation phenomena with respect to higher dimensional cylinders are more mysterious. In fact, it seems for instance that not even a single explicit example of a pair of non-isomorphic varieties XX and YY which fail the 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}-cancellation property in a minimal way, in the sense that X×𝔸2X\times\mathbb{A}^{2} and Y×𝔸2Y\times\mathbb{A}^{2} are isomorphic while X×𝔸1X\times\mathbb{A}^{1} and Y×𝔸1Y\times\mathbb{A}^{1} are still non isomorphic, is known so far. In this article, we fill this gap by constructing a positive dimensional moduli of smooth affine surfaces which fail the 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}-cancellation property minimally. That such varieties exist was certainly a natural expectation, and their existence is therefore neither really surprising, nor probably exciting in itself due to the abundance of simpler counter-examples to the cancellation problem. Their interest lies rather in the fact that they provide additional insight on the algebro-geometric properties that a variety should satisfy in order to fail cancellation.

Indeed, it follows from Iitaka-Fujita strong Cancellation Theorem [9] that a smooth affine variety XX which fails cancellation has negative logarithmic Kodaira dimension, a property conjecturally equivalent in dimension higher or equal to 33 to the fact that XX is covered by images of the affine line and equivalent for surfaces to the existence of an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration π:X→C\pi:X\rightarrow C over a smooth curve [12], i.e. a flat fibration with general fibers isomorphic to the affine line. In the particular case of the cancellation problem for 11-dimensional cylinders, a further striking discovery of Makar-Limanov is that the existence of nontrivial actions of the additive group 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a} on XX is a necessary condition for non-cancellation. Namely, Makar-Limanov semi-rigidity theorem [11] (see also [5, Proposition 9.23]) asserts that if XX is rigid, i.e. does not admit any nontrivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action, then the projection prX:X×𝔸1→X\mathrm{pr}_{X}:X\times\mathbb{A}^{1}\rightarrow X is invariant under all 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions on XX. As a consequence, if either XX or YY is rigid then every isomorphism between X×𝔸1X\times\mathbb{A}^{1} and Y×𝔸1Y\times\mathbb{A}^{1} descends to an isomorphism between XX and YY. Combined with Fieseler’s topological description of algebraic quotient morphisms of 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions on smooth complex affine surfaces [4], these results imply that a smooth affine surface which fails 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cancellation must admit a nontrivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action whose algebraic quotient morphism π:X→X//𝔾a=Spec(Γ(X,𝒪X)𝔾a)\pi:X\rightarrow X/\!/\mathbb{G}_{a}=\mathrm{Spec}(\Gamma(X,\mathcal{O}_{X})^{\mathbb{G}_{a}}) is not a locally trivial 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle. This holds of course for the two smooth surfaces x​z−y⁡(y+1)=0xz-y(y+1)=0 and x2​z−y⁡(y+1)=0x^{2}z-y(y+1)=0 used by Danielewski in his celebrated counter-example, showing a posteriori that his construction was essentially optimal in this dimension. The rich families of existing counter-examples to 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cancellation in dimension 22 lend support to the conjecture that every smooth affine surface which is neither rigid nor isomorphic to the total space of line bundle over an affine curve fails the 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cancellation property.

In view of this conjecture, a smooth affine surface XX which fails the 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}-cancellation property in a minimal way must be simultaneously rigid and equipped with an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration π:X→C\pi:X\rightarrow C over a smooth curve, and the well known fact that 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations over affine curves are algebraic quotient morphisms of nontrivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions implies further that CC must be projective. This is precisely the case for the family of surfaces we construct in this article, a particular example being the smooth affine cubic surfaces

X={(−1+α23x2+α23x3)3+8(x13+x23+x33)=0}and X′={(−1+2αx1+α23x2+α23x3)3+8(x13+x23+x33)=0}X=\{(-1+\alpha\sqrt[3]{2}x_{2}+\alpha\sqrt[3]{2}x_{3})^{3}+8(x_{1}^{3}+x_{2}^{3}+x_{3}^{3})=0\}\;\textrm{and\;}X^{\prime}=\{(-1+2\alpha x_{1}+\alpha\sqrt[3]{2}x_{2}+\alpha\sqrt[3]{2}x_{3})^{3}+8(x_{1}^{3}+x_{2}^{3}+x_{3}^{3})=0\}

in 𝔸3=Spec⁡(ℂ⁡[x1,x2,x3])\mathbb{A}^{3}=\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}]), where α=exp⁡(i​π/3)\alpha=\exp(i\pi/3), which are both rigid and equipped with an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration over ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}. These arise as the complements in the Fermat cubic surface V={x03+x13+x23+x33=0}V=\{x_{0}^{3}+x_{1}^{3}+x_{2}^{3}+x_{3}^{3}=0\} in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} of the plane cuspidal cubics C={−(x2+x3)3+4​(x13+x23+x33)}=0C=\{-(x_{2}+x_{3})^{3}+4(x_{1}^{3}+x_{2}^{3}+x_{3}^{3})\}=0 and C′={−((23)2x1+x2+x3)3+4(x13+x23+x33)=0}C^{\prime}=\{-((\sqrt[3]{2})^{2}x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3})^{3}+4(x_{1}^{3}+x_{2}^{3}+x_{3}^{3})=0\} obtained by intersecting VV with its tangent hyperplane at the points p=[α23:0:1:1]p=[\alpha\sqrt[3]{2}:0:1:1] and p′=[α23:23:−1:1]p^{\prime}=[\alpha\sqrt[3]{2}:\sqrt[3]{2}:-1:1] respectively. The group of automorphisms of VV being isomorphic to ℤ3×𝔖4\mathbb{Z}_{3}\times\mathfrak{S}_{4}, where ℤ3\mathbb{Z}_{3} is the 3-torsion subgroup of PGL⁡(4,ℂ)\mathrm{PGL(4;\mathbb{C})} and where 𝔖4\mathfrak{S}_{4} denotes the group of permutations of the variables, the fact that pp and p′p^{\prime} do not belong to a same Aut⁡(V)\mathrm{Aut}(V)-orbit implies that the pairs (V,C)(V,C) and (V,C′)(V,C^{\prime}) are not isomorphic. Our main result just below then implies in turn that XX and X′X^{\prime} are non isomorphic, with isomorphic 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}-cylinders X×𝔸2X\times\mathbb{A}^{2} and X′×𝔸2X^{\prime}\times\mathbb{A}^{2}.

Theorem.

Let (Vi,Ci)(V_{i},C_{i}), i=1,2i=1,2, be non isomorphic pairs consisting of a smooth cubic surface Vi⊂ℙ3V_{i}\subset\mathbb{P}^{3} and a cuspidal hyperplane section Ci=Vi∩HiC_{i}=V_{i}\cap H_{i}. Then the affine surfaces Xi=Vi∖CiX_{i}=V_{i}\setminus C_{i} are non isomorphic, with non isomorphic 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cylinders Xi×𝔸1X_{i}\times\mathbb{A}^{1} but with isomorphic 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}-cylinders Xi×𝔸2X_{i}\times\mathbb{A}^{2}, i=1,2i=1,2.

As a consequence, all smooth affine surfaces arising as complements of cuspidal hyperplane sections of smooth projective cubic surfaces have isomorphic 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}-cylinders. Noting that the projective closure in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} of the surface X0⊂𝔸3=Spec⁡(ℂ⁡[x,y,z])X_{0}\subset\mathbb{A}^{3}=\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[x,y,z]) with equation x2​y+y2+z3+1=0x^{2}y+y^{2}+z^{3}+1=0 is a smooth cubic surface intersecting the plane at infinity along the cuspidal cubic x2​y+z3=0x^{2}y+z^{3}=0, we obtain the following:

Corollary.

Let XX be a smooth affine surface isomorphic to the complement of a cuspidal hyperplane section of a smooth projective cubic surface. Then X×𝔸2X\times\mathbb{A}^{2} is isomorphic to the affine cubic fourfold Z⊂𝔸5=Spec⁡(ℂ⁡[x,y,z]​[u,v])Z\subset\mathbb{A}^{5}=\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[x,y,z][u,v]) with equation x2​y+y2+z3+1=0x^{2}y+y^{2}+z^{3}+1=0. Furthermore, XX is isomorphic to the geometric quotient of a proper action of the group 𝔾a2\mathbb{G}_{a}^{2} on ZZ.

The scheme of the proof of the Theorem given in the next section is the following. The fact that the affine surfaces X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} are non-isomorphic follows from the non-isomorphy of the pairs (V1,C1)(V_{1},C_{1}) and (V2,C2)(V_{2},C_{2}) via an argument of classical birational geometry of projective cubic surfaces, which simultaneously renders the conclusion that X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} are rigid. The non isomorphy of the cylinders X1×𝔸1X_{1}\times\mathbb{A}^{1} and X2×𝔸1X_{2}\times\mathbb{A}^{1} is then a straightforward consequence Makar-Limanov’s semi-rigidity Theorem.

The existence of an isomorphism between the 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}-cylinders X1×𝔸2X_{1}\times\mathbb{A}^{2} and X2×𝔸2X_{2}\times\mathbb{A}^{2} is derived in two steps: the first one consists of another instance of a Danielewski fiber product trick argument, which provides a smooth affine threefold WW equipped with simultaneous structures of line bundles π1:W→X1\pi_{1}:W\rightarrow X_{1} and π2:W→X2\pi_{2}:W\rightarrow X_{2} over X1X_{1} and X2X_{2}. But here, in contrast with the situation in Danielewski’s counter-example, the fact that the 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cylinders over X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} are not isomorphic implies that these two line bundles cannot be simultaneously trivial. Nevertheless, the crucial observation which enables a second step, reminiscent to Hochster construction, is that the pull-backs via the isomorphisms πi∗:Pic⁡(Xi)→Pic⁡(W)\pi_{i}^{*}:\mathrm{Pic}(X_{i})\rightarrow\mathrm{Pic}(W) of the classes of these lines bundles in the Picard groups of X1X_{1} and X2X_{2}, say L1L_{1} and L2L_{2}, coincide. Letting q:E→Wq:E\rightarrow W be a line bundle representing the common inverse in Pic⁡(W)\mathrm{Pic}(W) of π1∗​L1=π2∗​L2\pi_{1}^{*}L_{1}=\pi_{2}^{*}L_{2}, the composition πi∘q:E→Xi\pi_{i}\circ q:E\rightarrow X_{i} is then a vector bundle of rank 22 isomorphic to the direct sum Li⊕Li∨L_{i}\oplus L_{i}^{\vee}, where Li∨L_{i}^{\vee} denotes the dual of LiL_{i}, hence isomorphic to det(E)⊕𝔸Xi1=(Li⊗Li∨)⊕𝔸Xi1≃𝔸Xi1⊕𝔸Xi1\det(E)\oplus\mathbb{A}_{X_{i}}^{1}=(L_{i}\otimes L_{i}^{\vee})\oplus\mathbb{A}_{X_{i}}^{1}\simeq\mathbb{A}_{X_{i}}^{1}\oplus\mathbb{A}_{X_{i}}^{1} by virtue of result of Pavaman Murthy [13] asserting that every vector bundle on a smooth affine surface birationaly equivalent to a ruled surface is isomorphic to the direct sum of a trivial bundle with a line bundle.

The construction of these isomorphisms suggests the following strengthening of the above conjecture characterizing smooth affine surfaces failing the 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cancellation property, which would settle the question of the behavior of smooth affine surfaces under stabilization by affine spaces:

Conjecture.

A smooth affine surface XX with negative logarithmic Kodaira dimension is either isomorphic to the total space of a line bundle over a curve, or it fails the 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}-cancellation property. Furthermore, every non rigid XX which fails the 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}-cancellation property also fails the 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cancellation property.

1. Proof of the theorem

1.1. Rigid affine cubic surfaces

Given a smooth cubic surface V⊂ℙ3V\subset\mathbb{P}^{3} and a hyperplane section V∩HV\cap H consisting of an irreducible plane cuspidal cubic CC, the restriction of the projection ℙ3⇢ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{3}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{2} from the singular point pp of CC induces a rational map V⇢ℙ2V\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{2} of degree 22 with pp as a unique proper base point. Its lift to the blow-up α:Y→V\alpha:Y\rightarrow V of VV at pp coincides with the morphism θ:Y→ℙ2\theta:Y\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{2} defined by the anti-canonical linear system |−KY||-K_{Y}| and it factors through a birational morphism Y→ZY\rightarrow Z to the anti-canonical model Z=Projℂ​(⨁m≥0H0​(Y,−m​KY))Z=\mathrm{Proj}_{\mathbb{C}}(\bigoplus_{m\geq 0}H^{0}(Y,-mK_{Y})) of YY, followed by a Galois double cover Z→ℙ2Z\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{2} ramified over a quartic curve. The nontrivial involution of the double cover Z→ℙ2Z\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{2} lifts to a biregular involution of YY exchanging the proper transform of CC and the exceptional divisor EE of α\alpha. This involution descends back to a birational map Gp:V⇢VG_{p}:V\dashrightarrow V, called the Geiser involution of VV with center at pp, which contracts CC to pp and restricts to a biregular involution jp:X→Xj_{p}:X\rightarrow X of the affine complement XX of CC in VV.

Lemma 1.

Let XiX_{i} be the complements of cuspidal hyperplanes sections Ci=Vi∩HiC_{i}=V_{i}\cap H_{i} with respective singular points pip_{i} of smooth cubic surfaces Vi⊂ℙ3V_{i}\subset\mathbb{P}^{3}, i=1,2i=1,2. Then for every isomorphism ψ:X1→∼X2\psi:X_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\rightarrow}}X_{2}, the birational map ψ¯:V1⇢V2\overline{\psi}:V_{1}\dashrightarrow V_{2} extending ψ\psi is either an isomorphism of pairs (V1,C1)→∼(V2,C2)(V_{1},C_{1})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\rightarrow}}(V_{2},C_{2}) or it factors in a unique way as the composition of the Geiser involution Gp1:V1⇢V1G_{p_{1}}:V_{1}\dashrightarrow V_{1} followed by an isomorphism of pairs (V1,C1)→∼(V2,C2)(V_{1},C_{1})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\rightarrow}}(V_{2},C_{2}). In particular, X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} are isomorphic if and only if so are the pairs (V1,C1)(V_{1},C_{1}) and (V2,C2)(V_{2},C_{2}).

Proof.

Letting αi:Yi→Vi\alpha_{i}:Y_{i}\rightarrow V_{i} be the blow-up of ViV_{i} at pip_{i}, with exceptional divisor EiE_{i}, XiX_{i} is isomorphic to Yi∖(Ci∪Ei)Y_{i}\setminus(C_{i}\cup E_{i}) where we identified CiC_{i} and its proper transform in YiY_{i}. The birational map ψ¯:V1⇢V2\overline{\psi}:V_{1}\dashrightarrow V_{2} lifts to a birational Ψ¯=α2−1∘ψ¯∘α1:Y1⇢Y2\overline{\Psi}=\alpha_{2}^{-1}\circ\overline{\psi}\circ\alpha_{1}:Y_{1}\dashrightarrow Y_{2} extending ψ\psi, and the assertion is equivalent to the fact that Ψ¯\overline{\Psi} is an isomorphism of pairs (Y1,C1∪E1)→∼(Y2,C2∪E2)(Y_{1},C_{1}\cup E_{1})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\rightarrow}}(Y_{2},C_{2}\cup E_{2}). Since Y1Y_{1} and Y2Y_{2} are smooth with the same Picard rank ρ⁡(Yi)=8\rho(Y_{i})=8, this holds provided that either Ψ¯\overline{\Psi} or Ψ¯−1\overline{\Psi}^{-1} is a morphism. So suppose for contradiction that Ψ¯\overline{\Psi} or Ψ¯−1\overline{\Psi}^{-1} are both strictly birational and let Y1←σ1W→σ2Y2Y_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sigma_{1}}}{{\leftarrow}}W\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sigma_{2}}}{{\rightarrow}}Y_{2} be the minimal resolution of Ψ¯\overline{\Psi}. Since Y1Y_{1} and Y2Y_{2} are smooth and Ψ¯\overline{\Psi} and Ψ¯−1\overline{\Psi}^{-1} are both strictly birational, σ1\sigma_{1} consists of a non-empty sequence of blow-ups of smooth points whose centers lie over C1∪E1C_{1}\cup E_{1}, while σ2\sigma_{2} is a non-empty sequence of contractions of successives (−1)(-1)-curves on WW supported on the total transform σ1−1​(C1∪E1)\sigma_{1}^{-1}(C_{1}\cup E_{1}) of C1∪E1C_{1}\cup E_{1}. Furthermore, the minimality assumption implies that the first curve contracted by σ2\sigma_{2} is the proper transform in WW of C1C_{1} or E1E_{1}. Since C1C_{1} and E1E_{1} are (−1)(-1)-curves in Y1Y_{1}, the only possibility is thus that all successive centers of σ1\sigma_{1} lie over E1∖C1E_{1}\setminus C_{1} (resp. C1∖E1C_{1}\setminus E_{1}) and that the first curve contracted by σ2\sigma_{2} is the proper transform of E1E_{1} (resp. OPENC1)C_{1}). But since C1C_{1} and E1E_{1} are tangent in Y1Y_{1}, so are their proper transforms in WW, and then the image of C1C_{1} (resp. OPENE1)E_{1}) by the contraction τ:W→W′\tau:W\rightarrow W^{\prime} of E1E_{1} (resp. C1C_{1}) factoring σ2:W→Y2\sigma_{2}:W\rightarrow Y_{2} would be singular. Since it cannot be contracted at any further step, its image by σ2\sigma_{2} would be a singular curve contained in Y2∖X2=C2∪E2Y_{2}\setminus X_{2}=C_{2}\cup E_{2}, which is absurd. ∎

Corollary 2.

Let XX be the complement of a cuspidal hyperplane section CC of a smooth cubic surface V⊂ℙ3V\subset\mathbb{P}^{3}. Then there exists a split exact sequence

0→Aut⁡(V,C)→Aut⁡(X)→{idX,jp}≃ℤ2→0,0\rightarrow\mathrm{Aut}(V,C)\rightarrow\mathrm{Aut}(X)\rightarrow\{\mathrm{id}_{X},j_{p}\}\simeq\mathbb{Z}_{2}\rightarrow 0,

where Aut⁡(V,C)\mathrm{Aut}(V,C) is the automorphism group of the pair (V,C)(V,C) and jp:X→∼Xj_{p}:X\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\rightarrow}}X is the biregular involution induced by the Geiser involution of VV with center at the singular point pp of CC. In particular, Aut⁡(X)\mathrm{Aut}(X) is a finite group, isomorphic to ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} for a general smooth cubic surface VV.

Proof.

We view Aut⁡(V,C)\mathrm{Aut}(V,C) as a subgroup of Aut⁡(X)\mathrm{Aut}(X) via the homomorphism which associates to every automorphism of VV preserving CC, hence XX, its restriction to XX. Since by virtue of the previous lemma, the extension of every automorphism φ\varphi of XX to a birational self-map φ¯:V⇢V\overline{\varphi}:V\dashrightarrow V is either an automorphism of the pair (V,C)(V,C) or the composition of the Geiser involution Gp:V⇢VG_{p}:V\dashrightarrow V with an automorphism of this pair, the first assertion follows. The second assertion is a consequence of the fact that the automorphism group Aut⁡(V)\mathrm{Aut}(V) of a smooth cubic surface VV is always finite, actually trivial for a general such surface. ∎

The following proposition provides the first part of the proof of the theorem:

Proposition 3.

Let XiX_{i} be the complements of cuspidal hyperplanes sections Ci=Vi∩HiC_{i}=V_{i}\cap H_{i} of smooth cubic surfaces Vi⊂ℙ3V_{i}\subset\mathbb{P}^{3}, i=1,2i=1,2. If the pairs (V1,C1)(V_{1},C_{1}) and (V2,C2)(V_{2},C_{2}) are not isomorphic then the 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cylinders X1×𝔸1X_{1}\times\mathbb{A}^{1} and X2×𝔸1X_{2}\times\mathbb{A}^{1} are not isomorphic.

Proof.

The rigidity of XiX_{i} asserted by Corollary 2 implies by virtue of [5, Proposition 9.23] that the Makar-Limanov invariant ML⁡(Xi×𝔸1)\mathrm{ML}(X_{i}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}) of Xi×𝔸1X_{i}\times\mathbb{A}^{1} is equal to the sub-algebra Γ⁡(Xi,𝒪Xi)\Gamma(X_{i},\mathcal{O}_{X_{i}}) of Γ⁡(Xi,𝒪Xi)​[t]=Γ⁡(Xi×𝔸1,𝒪Xi×𝔸1)\Gamma(X_{i},\mathcal{O}_{X_{i}})[t]=\Gamma(X_{i}\times\mathbb{A}^{1},\mathcal{O}_{X_{i}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}}). Since every isomorphism between two algebras induces an isomorphism between their Makar-Limanov invariants, it follows that every isomorphism X1×𝔸1→∼X2×𝔸1X_{1}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\rightarrow}}X_{2}\times\mathbb{A}^{1} descends to a unique isomorphism ψ:X1→∼X2\psi:X_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\rightarrow}}X_{2} making the following diagram commutative

On the other hand, the hypothesis that the pairs (V1,C1)(V_{1},C_{1}) and (V2,C2)(V_{2},C_{2}) are not isomorphic combined with Lemma 1, implies that X1X_{1} is not isomorphic to X2X_{2} and so, X1×𝔸1X_{1}\times\mathbb{A}^{1} is not isomorphic to X2×𝔸1X_{2}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}. ∎

1.2. Isomorphisms between 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}-cylinders

As explained above, the first step of the construction is a Danielewski fiber product trick creating a smooth affine threefold WW which is simultaneously the total space of a line bundle over X1X_{1} and X2X_{2}. To setup such a fiber product argument, we first construct a certain smooth algebraic space δ:B→ℙ1\delta:B\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} with the property that every complement XX of an irreducible cuspidal hyperplane section CC of a smooth cubic surface V⊂ℙ3V\subset\mathbb{P}^{3} admits the structure of an étale locally trivial 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle ρ:X→B\rho:X\rightarrow B.

1.2.1.

Letting ℙ1=Proj⁡(ℂ⁡[z0,z1])\mathbb{P}^{1}=\mathrm{Proj}(\mathbb{C}[z_{0},z_{1}]), the algebraic space δ:B→ℙ1\delta:B\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} is obtained by the following gluing procedure:

1.2.2.

Since the automorphism group of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} is the affine group Aff1=𝔾m⋉𝔾a\mathrm{Aff}_{1}=\mathbb{G}_{m}\ltimes\mathbb{G}_{a}, every étale locally trivial 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle ρ:S→B\rho:S\rightarrow B is an affine-linear bundle whose isomorphy class is determined by an element in the non-abelian cohomology group He´​t1​(B,Aff1)H_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}^{1}(B,\mathrm{Aff}_{1}). Equivalently ρ:S→B\rho:S\rightarrow B is a principal homogeneous bundle under the action of a line bundle L→BL\rightarrow B, considered as a locally constant group scheme over BB for the group law induced by the addition of germs of sections, whose class in Pic⁡(B)≃He´​t1​(B,𝔾m)\mathrm{Pic}(B)\simeq H_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}^{1}(B,\mathbb{G}_{m}) coincides with the image of the isomorphy class of ρ:S→B\rho:S\rightarrow B in He´​t1​(B,Aff1)H_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}^{1}(B,\mathrm{Aff}_{1}) by the map He´​t1​(B,Aff1)→He´​t1​(B,𝔾m)H_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}^{1}(B,\mathrm{Aff}_{1})\rightarrow H_{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}^{1}(B,\mathbb{G}_{m}) in the long exact sequence of non-abelian cohomology

Proposition 5.

The complement XX of a cuspidal hyperplane section CC of a smooth cubic surface V⊂ℙ3V\subset\mathbb{P}^{3} admits an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration f:X→ℙ1f:X\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} which factors through a principal homogeneous bundle ρ:X→B\rho:X\rightarrow B under the action of the cotangent line bundle γ:ΩB1→B\gamma:\Omega_{B}^{1}\rightarrow B of BB.

Proof.

Since CC is an anti-canonical divisor on VV, it follows from adjunction formula that every line on VV intersects CC transversally in a unique point. The image of CC by the contraction τ:V→ℙ2\tau:V\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{2} of any 66-tuple of disjoint lines, L1,…,L6L_{1},\ldots,L_{6}, on VV is therefore a rational cuspidal cubic containing the images qi=τ⁡(Li)q_{i}=\tau(L_{i}), i=1,…,6i=1,\ldots,6, in its regular locus. The rational pencil ℙ2⇢ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{2}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} generated by τ⁡(C)\tau(C) and three times its tangent line TT at its singular point lifts to a rational pencil f¯:V⇢ℙ1\overline{f}:V\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} whose restriction to XX is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration f:X→ℙ1f:X\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} with two degenerate fibers: one irreducible of multiplicity three consisting of the intersection of the proper transform of TT with XX, and a reduced one consisting of the disjoint union of the curves Li∩X≃𝔸1L_{i}\cap X\simeq\mathbb{A}^{1}, i=1,…,6i=1,\ldots,6. Choosing homogeneous coordinates [z0:z1][z_{0}:z_{1}] on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} in such a way that 00 and ∞\infty are the respective images of TT and CC by f¯\overline{f}, the same argument as in [3, §4] implies that f:X→ℙ1f:X\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} factors through an étale locally trivial 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle ρ:X→B\rho:X\rightarrow B. Letting γ:L→B\gamma:L\rightarrow B be the line bundle under which ρ:X→B\rho:X\rightarrow B becomes a principal homogeneous bundle, it follows from the relative cotangent exact sequence

0→ρ∗​ΩB1→ΩX1→ΩX/B1≃ρ∗​L∨→00\rightarrow\rho^{*}\Omega_{B}^{1}\rightarrow\Omega_{X}^{1}\rightarrow\Omega_{X/B}^{1}\simeq\rho^{*}L^{\vee}\rightarrow 0

of ρ\rho that detΩX1≃ρ∗​(ΩB1⊗L∨)\det\Omega_{X}^{1}\simeq\rho^{*}(\Omega_{B}^{1}\otimes L^{\vee}). Since detΩX1\det\Omega_{X}^{1} is trivial as CC is an anti-canonical divisor on VV and since ρ∗:Pic⁡(B)→Pic⁡(X)\rho^{*}:\mathrm{Pic}(B)\rightarrow\mathrm{Pic}(X) is an isomorphism because ρ:X→B\rho:X\rightarrow B is a locally trivial 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle, we conclude that L≃ΩB1L\simeq\Omega_{B}^{1}. ∎

The Picard group Pic⁡(B)\mathrm{Pic}(B) of BB is thus isomorphic to ℤ6\mathbb{Z}^{6} generated by the classes of the lines bundle 𝒪B​(p0)\mathcal{O}_{B}(p_{0}), 𝒪B​(∞i)\mathcal{O}_{B}(\infty_{i}), i=1,…,6i=1,\ldots,6, with the unique relation 𝒪B​(3​p0)=𝒪B​(∑i=16∞i)\mathcal{O}_{B}(3p_{0})=\mathcal{O}_{B}(\sum_{i=1}^{6}\infty_{i}). Example 7.

Let V⊂ℙ3V\subset\mathbb{P}^{3} be a general smooth cubic surface and let Δ⊂V\Delta\subset V be the curve consisting of points pp of VV at which the projective tangent hyperplane Tp​V⊂ℙ3T_{p}V\subset\mathbb{P}^{3} of VV at pp intersects VV along a cuspidal cubic. Let 𝒱=Δ×V\mathcal{V}=\Delta\times V and let 𝒞⊂𝒱\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{V} be relatively ample Cartier divisor with respect to prΔ:𝒱→Δ\mathrm{pr}_{\Delta}:\mathcal{V}\rightarrow\Delta whose fiber 𝒞p\mathcal{C}_{p} over every point p∈Δp\in\Delta is equal to the intersection Cp=V∩Tp​VC_{p}=V\cap T_{p}V. Since Aut⁡(V)\mathrm{Aut}(V) is trivial, the pairs (V,Cp)(V,C_{p}), p∈Δp\in\Delta, are pairwise non isomorphic, and so Θ=prΔ∣𝒳:𝒳=𝒱∖𝒞→Δ\Theta=\mathrm{pr}_{\Delta}\mid_{\mathcal{X}}:\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{V}\setminus\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\Delta is a family of pairwise non isomorphic rigid smooth affine surfaces whose 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}-cylinders are all isomorphic.

Remark 8.

The 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}-cylinder X×𝔸2X\times\mathbb{A}^{2} over the complement XX of a cuspidal hyperplane section CC of a smooth cubic surface VV is flexible in codimension 11, that is, for every closed point pp outside a possible empty closed subset Z⊂X×𝔸2Z\subset X\times\mathbb{A}^{2} of codimension at least two, the tangent space TX×𝔸2,pT_{X\times\mathbb{A}^{2},p} of X×𝔸2X\times\mathbb{A}^{2} at pp is spanned by tangent vectors to orbits of algebraic 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions on X×𝔸2X\times\mathbb{A}^{2}. This can be seen as follows: one first constructs by a similar procedure as in [3, §3.2] a flexible mate SS for XX, in the form of smooth affine surface flexible in codimension 11 admitting an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration π:S→ℙ1\pi:S\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} which factors through a principal homogeneous bundle π~:S→B\tilde{\pi}:S\rightarrow B under the action of a certain line bundle γ′:L→B\gamma^{\prime}:L\rightarrow B. The fiber product S×BXS\times_{B}X is then a smooth affine threefold which is simultaneously isomorphic to the total spaces of the line bundles π~∗​ΩB1\tilde{\pi}^{*}\Omega_{B}^{1} and ρ∗​L\rho^{*}L over SS and XX via the first and second projection respectively. Since SS is flexible in codimension 11, it follows from [3, Lemma 2.3] that S×BXS\times_{B}X and the total space F→S×BXF\rightarrow S\times_{B}X of the pull-back of L∨L^{\vee} by the morphism π~∘prS=ρ∘prX\tilde{\pi}\circ\mathrm{pr}_{S}=\rho\circ\mathrm{pr}_{X} are both flexible in codimension 11. By construction, FF is a vector bundle of rank 22 over XX, isomorphic to ρ∗​(L⊕L∨)\rho^{*}(L\oplus L^{\vee}) hence to the trivial vector bundle X×𝔸2X\times\mathbb{A}^{2} by virtue of [13, Theorem 3.1].
